name: Panax notoginseng (sanqi)
short: Case reports: oesophageal haematoma after capsules (cause unstated) or hirudin mix; pustular rash after saponin injection. Rats: more warfarin effect. Stroke trial, extract: serious events as placebo.
text: In a placebo-controlled randomised trial in China in 3072 adults with ischaemic stroke, who took a Panax notoginseng saponin extract or placebo by mouth for 3 months, serious adverse events occurred in 15 of 1488 patients (1.0%) given the extract and 16 of 1482 (1.1%) in the control group. A case series describes four elderly patients who developed a pustular drug eruption with fever and raised neutrophil counts after Panax notoginseng saponin injection (an injected extract, not the root taken by mouth), and the reaction required high-dose, long-term glucocorticoid therapy. Two case reports describe bleeding within the wall of the oesophagus (submucosal haematoma): in a 57-year-old woman whose symptoms began the day after she took 5 notoginseng capsules, which the authors' title calls spontaneous and the abstract does not attribute to the herb, and in a 60-year-old man with coronary heart disease and coronary stents who took a homemade mixture of hirudin and notoginseng powder, which the authors state caused it; both recovered. On interactions, a study in rats found that notoginseng saponins given with warfarin increased the prothrombin time and INR at all three doses and raised warfarin exposure (area under the curve) significantly at the medium and high doses, while the rises in warfarin blood concentration were not statistically significant; the saponins lowered expression of the liver enzyme CYP3A4 in the rats and in a laboratory cell line, and the authors concluded that they can increase warfarin's blood concentration and enhance its anticoagulant effect by inhibiting the expression of CYP3A4; a review of in vivo and in vitro studies states that notoginseng alters the handling of other drugs by regulating cytochrome P450 enzymes and P-glycoprotein, calling this a red flag for drugs with a narrow therapeutic window. A meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials (2216 patients with coronary heart disease or ischaemic stroke) found that notoginseng preparations added to aspirin inhibited platelet aggregation more than aspirin alone; preparations of one saponin type (panaxatriol saponins) also prolonged clotting times (prothrombin time and INR) more than aspirin alone, with no significant difference in bleeding-related events reported for that type, and gastrointestinal side effects and urticaria did not differ from aspirin alone; the authors concluded that the combination might produce stronger antiplatelet and anticoagulation effects without increasing bleeding risk.
